intro: Metrics tell you a service is slow; profiling tells you why. This lesson gives you the one model that explains most GPU performance questions, the roofline, and uses it to show exactly why decode is memory-bound and prefill is compute-bound, and when batching flips decode from one to the other. Then it covers the measuring tools in order of depth: nvidia-smi for a glance, DCGM metrics for fleets, Nsight Systems for timelines, and Nsight Compute for individual kernels.
objectives: Compute arithmetic intensity and the ridge point of a GPU
Use the roofline to classify a workload as compute-bound or memory-bound
Predict how batch size changes decode from memory-bound toward compute-bound
Choose between nvidia-smi, DCGM, Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute for a question
Read GPU timeline gaps that point to CPU, synchronisation or communication stalls

blocks.text: Every piece of GPU work does some floating-point operations (FLOPs) and moves some bytes to and from memory. Its **arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved. A GPU has a peak compute rate (FLOP/s) and a peak memory bandwidth (bytes/s); their ratio is the **ridge point**. Work with intensity below the ridge cannot use all the compute because memory cannot feed it fast enough: it is **memory-bound**. Work above the ridge is **compute-bound**.

blocks.caption: The roofline in numbers (an example GPU, not a specific product)
blocks.code:
peak compute   = 1,000 TFLOP/s  (dense FP16 Tensor Core)
peak bandwidth = 3.3 TB/s
ridge point    = 1,000e12 / 3.3e12 ~ 300 FLOPs per byte

attainable FLOP/s = min(peak compute, intensity x peak bandwidth)

blocks.text: Plot attainable performance against intensity on log axes and you get a slanted line (bandwidth-limited) meeting a flat roof (compute-limited) at the ridge. Every optimisation either raises a kernel's intensity, moving it right toward the roof, or makes it run closer to the line it is already under.

sections.heading: Placing prefill and decode on the roofline

blocks.text: A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token. In FP16 each parameter is 2 bytes. During **decode at batch size B**, the weights are read once and used for B tokens, so intensity is roughly 2B FLOPs over 2 bytes, about **B FLOPs per byte**. At batch 1 that is about 1, far below a ridge of around 300: the GPU uses well under 1% of its compute. At batch 64 it is about 64: much better, still memory-bound. Reading the KV cache adds bytes without many FLOPs, so long contexts push decode further toward the memory side.

**Prefill** of a 2,000-token prompt uses each weight for 2,000 tokens, an intensity in the thousands, well past the ridge: compute-bound. That is the roofline explanation of everything in the lifecycle lesson, and it predicts what helps: for decode, bigger batches, fewer bytes per weight (quantization) and faster memory; for prefill, more Tensor Core throughput and less redundant work (prefix caching).

Quantizing weights to FP8 halves the bytes per parameter, which both halves memory traffic and doubles intensity. That is why it speeds up memory-bound decode almost proportionally, even before faster FP8 Tensor Core maths is counted.

sections.heading: Measuring: from a glance to a kernel

rows: Is the GPU busy at all? Memory used? Throttling?
Per-GPU utilisation, Tensor Core and memory activity over time, across a fleet
Timeline: where time goes across CPU threads, CUDA kernels, memory copies, NCCL
Why one kernel is slow: achieved bandwidth and FLOPs versus peak

blocks.text: DCGM's profiling metrics are the useful upgrade over nvidia-smi's coarse utilisation: `DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE` shows how busy the Tensor Cores really are, and `DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE` shows how busy the memory interface is. A decode-heavy server typically shows DRAM activity high and Tensor activity low, the memory-bound signature in production. Some fields, such as SM activity, are commented out in the exporter's default counter list and must be enabled.

blocks.caption: Profile a short benchmark with Nsight Systems, then one kernel with Nsight Compute
blocks.code:
# timeline of CPU threads, CUDA kernels, memory copies and NCCL calls
nsys profile -o decode_run --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt python bench.py
nsys stats decode_run.nsys-rep

# detailed counters for the first 5 matmul-like kernels
ncu --kernel-name regex:gemm --launch-count 5 --set full -o gemm python bench.py

items: **Gaps between kernels** on the GPU row with CPU activity at the same moment: the CPU is too slow to launch work (scheduling, tokenization, Python overhead). Engines use CUDA graphs to cut launch overhead for exactly this reason.
**Long memory copies** between host and device in the steady state: something is being moved over PCIe each step that should stay on the GPU.
**NCCL kernels taking a large share** of each step in a multi-GPU run: communication is the bottleneck, covered in the parallelism stage.
**One kernel dominating**: profile it with Nsight Compute and compare achieved memory bandwidth with the GPU's peak. Near peak means it is already as fast as the hardware allows at that intensity.

blocks.text: Profile short, representative runs. A few seconds of steady-state decode at your real batch size tells you more than an hour of traces, and Nsight output for long runs gets unwieldy fast.

practice.title: Find the roofline in your own benchmark
steps: Look up your GPU's dense FP16 Tensor Core TFLOPS and memory bandwidth and compute its ridge point.
Compute the decode arithmetic intensity at batch 1, 8, 32 and 128 using the B FLOPs per byte rule, and mark which side of the ridge each falls on.
Run a decode benchmark at those batch sizes (vLLM's offline LLM class or `vllm bench serve` at matching concurrency) and record tokens per second.
Plot tokens per second against batch size; note where gains start to flatten.
Run `nsys profile` on a few seconds of steady-state decode and look for gaps between kernels and the share of time in matmul kernels.
If dcgm-exporter is available, watch DRAM_ACTIVE and PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE during the run and relate them to your roofline prediction.

focus: Intensity = FLOPs / bytes; ridge = peak FLOP/s / peak bytes/s.
Below the ridge: memory-bound. Above: compute-bound.
Decode intensity is about the batch size; prefill intensity is about the prompt length.
Quantization halves bytes and doubles intensity: big win for decode.
nvidia-smi for a glance, DCGM for fleets, nsys for timelines, ncu for kernels.
Timeline gaps usually mean the CPU or synchronisation, not the GPU.

items.desc: About batch size FLOPs per byte
Summaries of kernels, copies, API calls
Quick rolling power, utilisation, clocks, memory
Share of cycles Tensor Cores are busy
Share of cycles memory interface is busy

pitfalls: Judging efficiency from nvidia-smi utilisation alone.
Expecting more TFLOPS to speed up batch-1 decode.
Profiling cold-start or warm-up instead of steady state.
Hour-long Nsight captures nobody can open, instead of short representative runs.
Ignoring KV-cache reads, which make long-context decode even more memory-bound.

quiz.q: A GPU offers 800 TFLOP/s and 2 TB/s of bandwidth. What is its ridge point?
quiz.explain: Ridge point = peak compute / peak bandwidth = 800e12 / 2e12 = 400 FLOPs per byte.

quiz.q: On that GPU, FP16 decode runs at batch size 16. Which regime is it in?
options: Memory-bound: intensity of about 16 is far below the ridge
quiz.explain: FP16 decode intensity is roughly the batch size, about 16 FLOPs per byte, far below a ridge of 400, so memory bandwidth limits it.

quiz.q: Why does FP8 weight quantization speed up decode almost proportionally?
options: It halves the bytes read per token in a memory-bound workload
It doubles the number of Tensor Cores on the GPU
It removes the need for a KV cache
It moves decode onto the CPU
quiz.explain: Decode is limited by bytes moved. Halving bytes per weight halves the traffic, so steps finish roughly twice as fast if memory was the limit.

quiz.q: An Nsight Systems timeline shows frequent idle gaps on the GPU row while one CPU thread is fully busy. What does that suggest?
options: The CPU cannot launch work fast enough and the GPU starves
The GPU is compute-bound on matmul kernels
quiz.explain: Idle GPU time aligned with a busy CPU thread means kernels are not being issued quickly enough, a CPU or launch-overhead bottleneck.

quiz.q: Which tool would you use to find out why one specific matmul kernel achieves low memory bandwidth?
quiz.explain: Nsight Compute collects detailed counters for individual kernels, including achieved bandwidth and compute versus peak; the others give whole-GPU or topology views.
